Limits to scalable evaluation at the frontier:
LLM as Judge won’t beat twice the data

Florian E. Dorner ††thanks: Corresponding author: florian.dorner@tuebingen.mpg.de Affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, Tübingen Affiliation: Tübingen AI Center Affiliation: ETH Zürich    Vivian Y. Nastl Affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, Tübingen Affiliation: Tübingen AI Center Affiliation: ETH Zürich    Moritz Hardt Affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, Tübingen Affiliation: Tübingen AI Center
Abstract

High quality annotations are increasingly a bottleneck in the explosively growing machine learning ecosystem. Scalable evaluation methods that avoid costly annotation have therefore become an important research ambition. Many hope to use strong existing models in lieu of costly labels to provide cheap model evaluations. Unfortunately, this method of using models as judges introduces biases, such as self-preferencing, that can distort model comparisons. An emerging family of debiasing tools promises to fix these issues by using a few high quality labels to debias a large number of model judgments. In this paper, we study how far such debiasing methods, in principle, can go. Our main result shows that when the judge is no more accurate than the evaluated model, no debiasing method can decrease the required amount of ground truth labels by more than half. Our result speaks to the severe limitations of the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm at the evaluation frontier where the goal is to assess newly released models that are possibly better than the judge. Through an empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that the sample size savings achievable in practice are even more modest than what our theoretical limit suggests. Along the way, our work provides new observations about debiasing methods for model evaluation, and points out promising avenues for future work.

1 Introduction

As large models continue to advance in their capabilities, it is increasingly challenging for human experts to evaluate newly released models. Expert data annotation is not only slow and costly. Traditional benchmarking also struggles to keep up with rapidly changing model capabilities across an expanding range of tasks. Yet, as models become more powerful, there is hope that models themselves could become powerful tools for scaling up evaluation. An intriguing idea is to use a strong existing model to provide judgments about other models. Such a “model-as-judge” could provide labels to classification instances, compare model outputs, and replace human annotators across a variety of tasks.

Already implemented in practice in numerous instances, the model-as-judge paradigm, however, runs into some roadblocks. When used as judges, models exhibit a range of biases that can skew model comparisons and result in misleading model rankings. Recently proposed debiasing methods, however, promise a compelling way forward. Using a small number of ground truth labels, these methods can potentially debias a large number of model predictions, thus restoring their utility for benchmarking purposes.

Scalable evaluation is most needed—and most challenging—at the evaluation frontier: Newly released models for which we have little intuition as of yet. What makes this case so challenging is that the new model is likely better than the judge in some ways. In this work, we address the question whether debiasing methods together with the model-as-judge paradigm can, in principle, provide an adequate solution to scalable evaluation at the frontier. However, our theory, supported by empirical evaluation, makes a sobering prediction: Whenever the judge model performs worse at its task than the evaluated model, the optimal debiasing method is no better than using twice the ground truth data. This shows that, although there is merit to debiasing, at the evaluation frontier its economic gains are not greater than a factor-two savings in annotation cost.

1.1 Our contributions

In our theoretical work we focus on a standard evaluation setup that encompasses classification, question answering, arena-style comparisons, and safety evaluations. Given an input xx, a model mm produces an output m⁡(x)m(x) that receives a binary ground-truth score s⁡(x,m⁡(x))s(x,m(x)). For example, in classification the accuracy score s⁡(x,m⁡(x))s(x,m(x)) is 11 if the model’s output m⁡(x)m(x) matches the ground-truth label y⁡(x)y(x) and 00 otherwise. A judge model provides a binary proxy score s~​(x,m​(x))\tilde{s}(x,m(x)). We imagine that obtaining ground-truth scores is costly and proxy scores are significantly cheaper.

For a fixed model mm, our goal is to estimate its true score 𝔼s​(x,m​(x)),\E s(x,m(x)), where the expectation is taken over an input drawn from a distribution. However due to judge bias, simply using cheap proxy scores s~\tilde{s} can lead to substantially distorted estimates. To motivate the issue, Figure 1 shows how proxy scores can cause highly misleading rankings of model performance.

Rather than solely relying on proxy scores, we assume that we have a small number nn of ground-truth scores ss sampled IID, in addition to a larger number NN of proxy scores s~\tilde{s}. A debiasing method is any estimator that provides an unbiased estimate of the true score from the sample of available proxy scores and ground truth scores. In particular, debiasing methods guarantee that ranking models by their estimated performance produces correct model rankings with high probability.

We focus on sample size savings in terms of the ground-truth scores ss that debiasing methods can achieve by making use of the proxy scores s~\tilde{s}.

  • •

    We first show that the best possible savings are determined by the Pearson correlation between ss and s~\tilde{s} (Theorem 5).

  • •

    Our main result (Theorem 6) then shows that this correlation is small whenever the judge model performs worse than the evaluated model. In that case the best possible outcome is an effective doubling of the number of samples ss, no matter how many samples of the proxy score s~\tilde{s} are available (Corollary 7). This result remains true in a slightly weaker sense, when we allow for the proxy s~\tilde{s} to be continuous rather than binary (Theorem 10).

  • •

    In experiments on MMLU and MT-Bench, we empirically confirm that sample size savings of more than a factor two are rare: We only observe them when current state-of-the-art models are used to judge substantially weaker models.

In addition, we show that the commonly reported agreement rate between the judge and the ground truth neither meaningfully restricts the judge bias, nor the sample size savings for debiasing methods.

2 Formal setup and motivation

In this section, we introduce the formal model we use to analyze the model-as-judge paradigm. We then provide empirical and theoretical evidence that judge bias can indeed cause model-as-judge to produce misleading results, even when judge models are quite accurate.

We focus our analysis on aggregated binary evaluations: Given a prompt xx, a model mm receives a binary score s⁡(x,m⁡(x))s(x,m(x)) depending on its output m⁡(x)m(x). As both model outputs and evaluation protocols can be non-deterministic, we treat s⁡(x,m⁡(x))s(x,m(x)) as a random variable, even when the prompt xx and model output m⁡(x)m(x) are fixed. The model mm is then evaluated based on its expected score 𝔼s​(X,m​(X))\E s(X,m(X)). Here, the expectation is taken over the prompt distribution X∼𝒟X\sim\mathcal{D}, as well as additional randomness in the scores s⁡(⋅,m⁡(⋅))s(\cdot,m(\cdot)) introduced by the evaluation protocol.

This setup covers several important benchmarking and evaluation settings:

  • •

    Accuracy in classification and Q&A benchmarks: Here, the prompt xx is an instance to be classified or a question to be answered. Letting m⁡(x)m(x) denote the model’s output on input x,x, the accuracy score s⁡(x,m)s(x,m) equals one whenever m⁡(x)m(x) equals the label y⁡(x)y(x).

  • •

    Arena-style benchmarks: In this setting xx is a prompt. We sample the model’s response m⁡(x)m(x) and the response m′​(x)m^{\prime}(x) of another randomly selected model m′m^{\prime}. The score s⁡(x,m)s(x,m) indicates whether m⁡(x)m(x) was judged to be a better response than m′​(x)m^{\prime}(x).

  • •

    Safety benchmarks: For this, the prompt xx is designed to potentially elicit unsafe behaviour. The score s⁡(x,m)s(x,m) indicates whether the model’s response m⁡(x)m(x) is safe.

In each of these settings, we can use a language model as a judge model to score models more cheaply than via ground truth evaluation. To do so, we compute a proxy score s~\tilde{s} with the help of the judge model. We assume that the proxy score is binary as well. In the classification setting, for example, the judge models could provide the labels for evaluation. The proxy score would then be the classification accuracy with respect to the judge model’s labels. In arena comparisons, the LLM could replace human raters. And in safety benchmarks, an LLM could evaluate the safety of model outputs. Although our motivation focuses on language models as the source of proxy scores, our formal work applies to any proxy score, e.g., scores provided by crowdworkers rather than experts.

Precisely modeling the specific relationship between xx, s⁡(x,m)s(x,m) and s~​(x,m)\tilde{s}(x,m) is generally infeasible: Even in the simplest case of classification, this would require a precise formal model of not just the judge’s prediction m~​(x)\tilde{m}(x), but also the relationship between xx and the correct labels y⁡(x)y(x). We therefore treat the scoring functions ss and s~\tilde{s} as black boxes, as is standard, and focus on the joint distribution of the two induced random variables s⁡(m):=s⁡(X,m)s(m):=s(X,m) and s~​(m):=s~​(X,m)\tilde{s}(m):=\tilde{s}(X,m).

As both scores s⁡(m)s(m) and s~​(m)\tilde{s}(m) are binary, we only require three parameters to specify their joint distribution:

b⁡(m)\displaystyle b(m) =ℙ{s(m)=1}\displaystyle=\Pr\{s(m)=1\}
p⁡(m)\displaystyle p(m) =ℙ{s~​(m)=s⁡(m)∣s⁡(m)=1}\displaystyle=\Pr\{\tilde{s}(m)=s(m)\mid s(m)=1\}
q⁡(m)\displaystyle q(m) =ℙ{s~​(m)=s⁡(m)∣s⁡(m)=0}\displaystyle=\Pr\{\tilde{s}(m)=s(m)\mid s(m)=0\}

Here, the parameter b⁡(m)b(m) represents the model’s expected real score 𝔼s​(m)\E s(m), while p⁡(m)p(m) represents the probability that the evaluations s⁡(m)s(m) and s~​(m)\tilde{s}(m) match, conditional on the score ss being equal to one (i.e., the true positive rate). Similarly, q⁡(m)q(m) represents the probability of s​(m)=s~​(m)s(m)=\tilde{s}(m) conditional on s⁡(m)=0s(m)=0 (i.e., the true negative rate).

2.1 Judge bias can strongly perturb model rankings

We argue that estimating the expected proxy score 𝔼s~​(m)\E\tilde{s}(m) instead of the real expected score 𝔼s​(m)\E s(m) is problematic for benchmarking. In the spirit of Salaudeen and Hardt (2024), a benchmark has two purposes: quantifying model performance and ranking models. In turn, a useful LLM judge should accurately estimate each model’s performance, and induce the same ranking of evaluated models as the ground truth. For the first goal, the main quantity of interest is the judge bias, defined as

JB(m)≔𝔼(s~​(m)−s⁡(m))=(1−q⁡(m))​(1−b⁡(m))−(1−p⁡(m))​b​(m).\bias(m)\coloneqq\E(\tilde{s}(m)-s(m))=\left(1-q(m)\right)\left(1-b(m)\right)-\left(1-p(m)\right)b(m)\,.

Whenever JB(m)\bias(m) has large magnitude, the proxy score s~\tilde{s} misrepresents the performance b⁡(m)b(m) of model mm, even with large sample sizes.

When it comes to ranking models, the relationship between judge bias JB\bias and model rankings is more subtle: If the judge bias JB(m)\bias(m) was constant across all models, rankings would be unaffected. However, JB(m)\bias(m) can strongly depend on the evaluated model mm. If JB(m)\bias(m) is positive for models with low performance, and negative for better performing models, using the score of the judge s~\tilde{s} can easily perturb model rankings. Our next proposition provides such an example inspired by empirical work. Specifically, real-world classifiers are not only highly similar to each other (Mania et al., 2019), Mania and Sra (2020) also observe that when one classifier is better than another on real data, it tends to be strictly better in a point-wise sense, for the most part. We therefore consider using a classifier mm to evaluate a set ℳ\mathcal{M} of strictly better classifiers. In that case, using the proxy evaluations s~\tilde{s} based on mm fully reverses the correct model ranking:

Proposition 1.

Consider a binary classifier m~\tilde{m} and a set of strictly better binary classifiers ℳ\mathcal{M} such that m~​(x)=y​(x)\tilde{m}(x)=y(x) implies mi​(x)=y​(x)m_{i}(x)=y(x) for all mi∈ℳm_{i}\in\mathcal{M}. Let 𝔼s​(mi)\E s(m_{i}) represent the accuracy of model mim_{i} evaluated on the correct labels, and 𝔼s~​(mi)\E\tilde{s}(m_{i}) its accuracy evaluated on predictions of model m~\tilde{m}. Then for mi,mj∈ℳm_{i},m_{j}\in\mathcal{M}, 𝔼s​(mi)>𝔼s​(mj)\E s(m_{i})>\E s(m_{j}) implies 𝔼s~​(mi)<𝔼s~​(mj)\E\tilde{s}(m_{i})<\E\tilde{s}(m_{j}).

We prove Proposition 1 in Appendix C.6. An illustration is provided in Figure 1(a). We use GPT-4 labels to evaluate Claude-Sonnet, as well as a set of (fictitious) models on MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021). The fictitious models are denoted as “Claude-Sonnet + xx” and designed to be strictly better than Claude. This is done by changing wrong predictions of Claude into correct ones until accuracy is improved by x%x\%. Figure 1(b) shows a more realistic setting, with LLaMa3-70b judging the top-10 MMLU models according to HELM (Liang et al., 2023). While the ranking is not fully reversed, it is strongly perturbed. This effect can also be observed in prior work: For MT-Bench, the ranking of the best models is not consistently preserved when using LLM judges (Zheng et al., 2024).

2.2 High agreement rate is insufficient for evaluation

The results from the previous subsection might appear surprising, considering the strong performance of the judge models: LLaMa3-70b has 79%79\% accuracy on MMLU, while GPT-4 has 84%84\%, and the models used in MT-Bench have 85%85\% agreement with expert annotators. Our next proposition explains how it is possible for model rankings to be strongly perturbed despite accurate judges. Before stating it, we need to formally define the agreement AG(m)\agg(m) between score ss and proxy score s~\tilde{s} as

AG(m)≔ℙ{s(m)=s~(m)}=b(m)p(m)+(1−b(m))q(m).\agg(m)\coloneqq\Pr\{s(m)=\tilde{s}(m)\}=b(m)p(m)+\left(1-b(m)\right)q(m).

In the classification setting, the judge model’s accuracy lower bounds the agreement AG(m)\agg(m): Clearly s​(x,m)=s~​(x,m)s(x,m)=\tilde{s}(x,m) whenever the judge model m~\tilde{m} is correct. But when there are more than two classes, we also get s​(x,m)=s~​(x,m)=0s(x,m)=\tilde{s}(x,m)=0 whenever the true label y⁡(x)y(x) and the predictions m⁡(x)m(x) and m~​(x)\tilde{m}(x) are all different from each other. In particular, this highlights that the agreement AG(m)\agg(m) can indeed depend on the evaluated model mm, rather than just the judge m~\tilde{m}. For binary classification, however, the agreement rate equals the judge model’s accuracy and is thus constant across evaluated models. Our next proposition now relates judge bias to agreement:

Proposition 2.

Fix any model score b⁡(m)b(m). Then for any rr with b⁡(m)≤r,b(m)\leq r, there are values of q⁡(m)q(m) and p⁡(m)p(m), such that AG(m)=r\agg(m)=r and we obtain positive judge bias JB(m)=1−r\bias(m)=1-r. Similarly, for any rr with 1−b⁡(m)≤r,1-b(m)\leq r, there are values of q⁡(m)q(m) and p⁡(m)p(m), such that AG(m)=r\agg(m)=r and we obtain negative judge bias JB(m)=r−1\bias(m)=r-1.

Proposition 2 shows that for agreement AG(m)=r\agg(m)=r, there can be a judge bias of 1−r1-r in either direction. This means that even if AG(m)=r\agg(m)=r was constant across models mm, we could only reliably rank models for which the true score 𝔼s​(m)\E s(m) differs by more than 2​(1−r)2(1-r). As it is common for state-of-the-art models to differ in performance by only low single digit percentages, without further assumptions an agreement rate above 99%99\% (for each evaluated model!) would be required to ensure (asymptotically) correct rankings. For a proof, see Appendix C.7.

3 Debiasing LLM judgments

In the previous section, we demonstrated how biased LLM judges can lead to strongly perturbed model rankings. This motivates the need for debiasing methods. We begin this section by discussing a simple sufficient condition to guarantee asymptotically correct rankings: Ensure that our estimates of 𝔼s​(m)\E s(m) are unbiased for all models mm. Statistical bias correction methods can make use of a large number of proxy scores and a smaller number of gold standard labels to construct an unbiased estimator. We discuss one such method in detail, and show that it is essentially optimal in terms of estimator variance. Afterwards we prove our main result, i.e., that LLM judges offer limited benefits for evaluating state-of-the-art models.

3.1 Uniformly controlling judge bias ensures correct rankings

We begin with a simple and natural sufficient condition for correct rankings. This is that all model evaluations are approximately unbiased. The next proposition shows that this, in fact, entails correct rankings in expectation and hence also with a sufficient amount of data.

Proposition 3.

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} be a finite set of models such that for any m,m′∈ℳm,m^{\prime}\in\mathcal{M}

|𝔼(s⁡(m))−𝔼(s⁡(m′))|≥ϵ.|\E(s(m))-\E(s(m^{\prime}))|\geq\epsilon.

Let θ^\hat{\theta} be an estimator for 𝔼s​(m)\E s(m) such that Varθ^​(m)\V\hat{\theta}(m) converges to zero in the dataset size. Then if |𝔼θ^​(m)−𝔼(s⁡(m))|<ϵ2|\E\hat{\theta}(m)-\E(s(m))|<\frac{\epsilon}{2} for all models mm, using θ^\hat{\theta} to rank models yields the correct ranking with high probability.

Proof.

By construction, 𝔼θ^​(m)\E\hat{\theta}(m) induces the same model rankings as 𝔼s​(m)\E s(m). Chebyshev’s inequality and a union bound imply correct rankings as Varθ^​(m)\V\hat{\theta}(m) goes to zero. ∎

Proposition 3 implies that if we could guarantee sufficiently small estimator bias, a large amount of proxy samples s~\tilde{s} would yield correct rankings with high probability. However, it is important for bias to be small for all evaluated models. In light of the worst-case results from Proposition 2, we cannot rely on this to be true when solely basing our estimates on the proxy scores s~\tilde{s}.

3.2 Background on Prediction Powered Inference

We next discuss how to leverage a small amount of ground truth samples ss to debias the proxy scores s~\tilde{s}. This yields an unbiased estimator θ^\hat{\theta} for 𝔼s\E s, and thus asymptotically correct model rankings.

Specifically, we follow the Prediction Powered Inference (PPI) framework (Angelopoulos et al., 2023a) and a method by Chaganty et al. (2018) that is equivalent in our case: Alongside a large IID sample of model judgments s~i​(m)=s~​(xi,m)\tilde{s}_{i}(m)=\tilde{s}(x_{i},m) for integer i∈[1,N+n]i\in[1,N+n], we assume access to the corresponding ground truth label sj​(m)=s⁡(xj,m)s_{j}(m)=s(x_{j},m) for a small subset of integer j∈[1,n]j\in[1,n]. With this, we can construct an unbiased estimator θ^P​P\hat{\theta}^{PP} for 𝔼s​(m)\E s(m) by using the small parallel sample to estimate JB(m)\bias(m), and subtracting it from our estimate of 𝔼s~​(m)\E\tilde{s}(m). The PPI estimator thus equals

θ^P​P=1N​∑i=n+1N+ns~i​(m)+1n​∑j=1n(sj​(m)−s~j​(m)).\hat{\theta}^{PP}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=n+1}^{N+n}\tilde{s}_{i}(m)+\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\left(s_{j}(m)-\tilde{s}_{j}(m)\right).

Clearly, the PPI estimator is unbiased

𝔼θ^PP=𝔼s~​(m)+𝔼s​(m)−𝔼s~​(m)=𝔼s​(m),\E\hat{\theta}^{PP}=\E\tilde{s}(m)+\E s(m)-\E\tilde{s}(m)=\E s(m),

and has variance

Varθ^PP=1NVars~(m)+1nVar(s~(m)−s(m)).\V\hat{\theta}^{PP}=\frac{1}{N}\V\tilde{s}(m)+\frac{1}{n}\V(\tilde{s}(m)-s(m)).

Whenever N≫nN\gg n, the first term on the right hand side is small. Moreover, when s⁡(m)s(m) and s~​(m)\tilde{s}(m) are strongly correlated, the second term is small. Assuming both, we have Varθ^PP<Varθ^GT\V\hat{\theta}^{PP}<\V\hat{\theta}^{GT}, where θ^G​T\hat{\theta}^{GT} is the ground-truth sample average estimator θ^G​T=1n​∑j=1nsj​(m).\hat{\theta}^{GT}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}s_{j}(m).

However if the correlation between s⁡(m)s(m) and s~​(m)\tilde{s}(m) is small, the inequality is reversed. This issue can be fixed by interpolating between the PPI estimator and the classical estimator (Chaganty et al., 2018; Angelopoulos et al., 2023b), setting

θ^λP​P=λ​θ^P​P+(1−λ)​θ^G​T.\hat{\theta}^{PP}_{\lambda}=\lambda\hat{\theta}^{PP}+(1-\lambda)\hat{\theta}^{GT}.

As a linear combination of unbiased estimators this remains unbiased, but we can now optimize over λ\lambda to minimize estimator variance. We obtain the optimum value λ∗=Cov(s(m),s~(m))/((1+nN)Vars~(m)).{\lambda^{*}=\Cov(s(m),\tilde{s}(m))/\left(\left(1+\frac{n}{N}\right)\V\tilde{s}\left(m\right)\right)}. At this λ\lambda, the estimator θ^λ∗P​P\hat{\theta}^{PP}_{\lambda^{*}}never increases variance compared to the classical ground truth estimator:

Varθ^λ∗PP=1nVars(m)−1n+n2NCov(s⁡(m),s~​(m))2Var(s~​(m))≤1nVars(m)=Varθ^GT.\V\hat{\theta}^{PP}_{\lambda^{*}}=\frac{1}{n}\V s(m)-\frac{1}{n+\frac{n^{2}}{N}}\frac{\Cov(s(m),\tilde{s}(m))^{2}}{\V(\tilde{s}(m))}\leq\frac{1}{n}\V s(m)=\V\hat{\theta}^{GT}.

In the following subsection, we discuss to what extent the PPI estimator θ^λ∗P​P\hat{\theta}^{PP}_{\lambda^{*}} can reduce variance or equivalently improve sample efficiency, compared to the ground truth estimator θ^G​T\hat{\theta}^{GT}.

3.3 The sample efficiency factor τ\tau

As the variance of θ^G​T\hat{\theta}^{GT} scales as Θ⁡(1/n)\Theta(1/n), using an estimator θ^\hat{\theta} with r=Varθ^Varθ^GTr=\frac{\V\hat{\theta}}{\V\hat{\theta}^{GT}} is equivalent to increasing the ground-truth sample size by a factor of

τ⁡(θ^)≔Varθ^GTVarθ^=1r.\tau(\hat{\theta})\coloneqq\frac{\V\hat{\theta}^{GT}}{\V\hat{\theta}}=\frac{1}{r}.

We call τ⁡(θ^)\tau(\hat{\theta}) the sample efficiency factor of the estimator θ^\hat{\theta}. It is our main quantity of interest. In order to ensure it is well-defined, we assume b⁡(m),p⁡(m),q⁡(m)∈(0,1)b(m),p(m),q(m)\in(0,1) for the remainder of the text. Our next proposition provides an upper bound on the sample efficiency factor τ⁡(θ^λ∗P​P)\tau(\hat{\theta}^{PP}_{\lambda^{*}}) of PPI, based on the squared Pearson correlation between ss and s~\tilde{s}:

Proposition 4.

The sample efficiency factor for the PPI estimator is upper bounded by

τ⁡(θ^λ∗P​P)≤11−ρ​(s⁡(m),s~​(m))2,\tau(\hat{\theta}^{PP}_{\lambda^{*}})\leq\frac{1}{1-\rho(s(m),\tilde{s}(m))^{2}},

where

ρ​(s⁡(m),s~​(m))2=b⁡(m)(1−b⁡(m))​(p⁡(m)−𝔼s~​(m))2𝔼s~​(m)​(1−𝔼s~​(m)).\rho(s(m),\tilde{s}(m))^{2}=\frac{b(m)}{(1-b(m))}\frac{(p(m)-\E\tilde{s}(m))^{2}}{\E\tilde{s}(m)(1-\E\tilde{s}(m))}.

This upper bound is large whenever ρ2\rho^{2} is large. However, the sample efficiency factor τ⁡(θ^λ∗P​P)\tau(\hat{\theta}^{PP}_{\lambda^{*}}) is finite unless we have perfect correlation ρ2=1\rho^{2}=1. For any correlation bounded away from 11, the proxy samples can only provide a constant factor improvement. Scaling them up without also scaling the number of ground truth samples has limited benefits. The proof can be found in Appendix C.8.

3.4 PPI is near-optimal for non-adaptive binary evaluation

The limited sample efficiency gains of PPI compared to the classical estimator raise the question whether we can find an unbiased estimator with lower variance. Given black-box estimators that do not model the prompt-conditional distribution ℙ[(s​(m),s~​(m))|x]\Pr[(s(m),\tilde{s}(m))|x] and access to NN IID samples of proxy scores s~​(m)\tilde{s}(m) and nn IID parallel samples (s​(m),s~​(m))(s(m),\tilde{s}(m)) we show that the answer is no:

Theorem 5.

Let Θ\Theta be the set of all unbiased estimators for 𝔼s​(m)\E s(m) that observe nn joint IID samples (s​(m),s~​(m))(s(m),\tilde{s}(m)) and NN IID proxy samples s~​(m)\tilde{s}(m) independent of the joint samples. Then, any θ^∈Θ\hat{\theta}\in\Theta fulfills the variance bound

Varθ^≥Varθ^λ∗PP.\V\hat{\theta}\geq\V\hat{\theta}^{PP}_{\lambda^{*}}\,.

This means that the sample efficiency factor of θ^\hat{\theta} is bounded by

τ⁡(θ^)≤maxθ^∈Θ⁡τ⁡(θ^)=τ⁡(θ^λ∗P​P)≤11−ρ​(s⁡(m),s~​(m))2.\tau(\hat{\theta})\leq\max_{\hat{\theta}\in\Theta}\tau(\hat{\theta})=\tau(\hat{\theta}^{PP}_{\lambda^{*}})\leq\frac{1}{1-\rho(s(m),\tilde{s}(m))^{2}}\,.

Theorem 5 follows from an application of the Cramér-Rao bound, combined with extensive algebraic manipulation that was assisted by a computer algebra system. Appendix C.1 has the details.

3.5 Limited gains for evaluating state-of-the-art models

With Theorem 5 at hand, we can analyze the best sample efficiency factor τ\tau an unbiased estimator with access to a random sample of nn ground truth scores s⁡(m)s(m) can achieve by making use of model judgments s~\tilde{s}. In this subsection, we focus on the evaluation of frontier models that outperform older models, including the models used to judge them. We use the evaluated model’s score b⁡(m)b(m) and the judge’s agreement rate AG(m)\agg(m) as indicators for the respective model’s capabilities. We focus on tasks for which performing and judging the task are of similar difficulty, such that these indicators are comparable. As a prime example, for binary classification, AG(m)\agg(m) equals the judge’s accuracy, while b⁡(m)b(m) equals the evaluated model’s accuracy.

We thus capture the evaluation of frontier models with the assumption that the evaluated model’s score b⁡(m)b(m) is larger than the judge’s agreement rate AG(m)\agg(m). The next theorem shows that the squared correlation ρ​(s⁡(m),s~​(m))2\rho(s(m),\tilde{s}(m))^{2} is at most one half in this setting.

Theorem 6.

Assume 0.5≤AG(m)≤b⁡(m)0.5\leq\agg(m)\leq b(m). Then,

ρ​(s⁡(m),s~​(m))2≤0.5.\rho(s(m),\tilde{s}(m))^{2}\leq 0.5.

We prove Theorem 6 in Appendix C.2. Combining Theorem 6 with Theorem 5 allows us to bound the sample efficiency gains that any unbiased estimator can achieve for evaluating frontier models:

Corollary 7.

Assume 0.5≤AG(m)≤b⁡(m)0.5\leq\agg(m)\leq b(m). Then,

τmax=maxθ^∈Θ⁡τ⁡(θ^)≤2.\tau_{\max}=\max_{\hat{\theta}\in\Theta}\tau(\hat{\theta})\leq 2.

Corollary 7 implies that when evaluating state-of-the-art models, the best we can expect from using LLM judges is a factor-two improvement in sample efficiency. This is unless the judge’s task is substantially easier than the evaluated model’s task.

3.6 High agreement rate is insufficient for sample efficiency gains

Theorem 6 holds for arbitrarily high levels of agreement. Therefore, the theorem shows that high agreement rates are not just insufficient for avoiding judge bias—they’re also insufficient for obtaining a meaningful sample efficiency factor τ\tau. Our next proposition goes a step further and shows that the agreement AG(m)\agg(m) does not provide any lower bound on the sample efficiency factor τ\tau, even when the judge bias JB(m)\bias(m) is zero.

Proposition 8.

For any agreement rate 0.5≤AG(m)<10.5\leq\agg(m)<1, there exist values of b⁡(m),p⁡(m),q⁡(m)∈(0,1)b(m),p(m),q(m)\in(0,1) such that

JB(m)=ρ​(s⁡(m),s~​(m))2=0​ and thus ​τmax=1.\bias(m)=\rho(s(m),\tilde{s}(m))^{2}=0\text{ and thus }\tau_{\max}=1.

We prove the proposition in Appendix C.9. It implies that in some cases despite access to s~\tilde{s}, no unbiased estimator has less variance than θ^G​T\hat{\theta}^{GT}. It might be surprising that there are cases in which we cannot make productive use of the proxy evaluations s~\tilde{s} despite zero judge bias. However, without further assumptions, JB(m)\bias(m) can vary wildly between models, so that we cannot skip estimating it anew for each model. Now, even if s~\tilde{s} has zero judge bias, the estimator does not “know” that, but rather has to estimate JB(m)\bias(m) from joint observations (s,s~)(s,\tilde{s}). In the configuration from the proposition, estimating the judge bias JB(m)\bias(m) turns out as hard as directly estimating the real score 𝔼s​(m)\E s(m).

3.7 Experiments

So far, we have shown that even optimal debiasing yields limited sample efficiency gains at the frontier (Section 3). In this section, we have a more detailed look into the sample efficiency gains on popular benchmarks that can be achieved by using current flagship models as judges.

Our experiments in this section focus on two settings: Multiple-choice question answering on MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021) and chatbot evaluation on MT-Bench (Zheng et al., 2024). Additional experiments on TruthfulQA can be found in Appendix B.2. In all cases, we calculate the empirical correlation ρ⁡(s,s~)\rho(s,\tilde{s}) between the score ss and the proxy s~\tilde{s} to obtain and plot an upper bound for the sample efficiency factor τmax\tau_{\max} based on Theorem 5.

We first focus on MMLU, a multiple-choice question answering benchmark for the world knowledge of language models. We obtain model predictions from the HELM (Liang et al., 2023) leaderboard. We then aggregate all subtasks of MMLU into a single test set and set ss to equal the accuracy score s⁡(x,m)=𝕀⁡(m⁡(x)=y⁡(x))s(x,m)=\mathbb{I}(m(x)=y(x)). Here 𝕀\mathbb{I} is the indicator function, m⁡(x)m(x) is the model’s answer and y⁡(x)y(x) is the correct answer. For model-based evaluations using m~\tilde{m} as a judge, we replace the correct answer y⁡(x)y(x) by the judge’s prediction m~​(x)\tilde{m}(x), setting s~​(x,m)=𝕀⁡(m⁡(x)=m~​(x))\tilde{s}(x,m)=\mathbb{I}(m(x)=\tilde{m}(x)).

In the second setting, we evaluate model performance on MT-Bench, an arena-style benchmark designed to evaluate the ability of models to follow instructions. The benchmark comes with results for six models. For each pair of these models mm and m′m^{\prime}, both models are queried with the same prompt xx. The test set for each model mm then consists of all triples of the form (m,m′,x)(m,m^{\prime},x), for other models in the benchmark m′m^{\prime} and prompts xx. For each triple in the test set, an expert evaluator decides, whether model mm produced a better response than m′m^{\prime}. In that case, the score s⁡(x,m)s(x,m) for model mm is one, otherwise it is zero. For the proxy score s~​(x,m)\tilde{s}(x,m) we replace the expert’s answer by the GPT-4 response provided by Zheng et al. (2024). For more details, consider Appendix B.

Figures 2 and 3 show the optimal sample efficiency factor τmax\tau_{\max} on MMLU and MT-Bench respectively. The sample efficiency factor τmax\tau_{\max} consistently stays below the value of two suggested by Corollary 7, except when current flagship models are used to judge the significantly worse LLama2-7b on MMLU. This exception is not surprising, as in that case AG≫b\agg\gg b such that the assumptions for Corollary 7 are heavily violated. Interestingly, τmax\tau_{\max} stays below two in all other cases, even when stronger models like GPT-4 are used to evaluate weaker models like LLaMa3-70b. This suggests that the upper bound on τmax\tau_{\max} from Corollary 7 is fairly robust. We also note that τmax\tau_{\max} is often substantially smaller than two, especially on MMLU. This highlights that Corollary 7 provides a best-case upper bound rather than a guarantee that τmax\tau_{\max} will be close to two in practice.

4 Going beyond binary evaluation

So far we have assumed the proxy score s~\tilde{s} to be binary. In this section, we relax this assumption. By not forcing the judge to fully commit to a single answer, we hope to obtain a more useful proxy s~\tilde{s}. For example, in a Q&A task, we can make use of the uncertainty of a judge model m′m^{\prime} by setting s~​(x,m)=ℙm′​(x)(m⁡(x))\tilde{s}(x,m)=\Pr_{m^{\prime}(x)}(m(x)) equal to the probability the judge m′m^{\prime} assigned to the model answer m⁡(x)m(x).

In terms of analysis, the non-parametric joint likelihood of (s,s~)(s,\tilde{s}) resulting from non-binary proxies makes it exceedingly hard to prove an analogue of Theorem 5 for all unbiased estimators. Instead, we focus on the PPI estimator, θ^λ∗P​P\hat{\theta}^{PP}_{\lambda^{*}}. It is a natural choice of estimator, given its proven optimality in the special case of binary proxies s~\tilde{s}. In order to state a condition similar to AG≤b\agg\leq b from Theorem 6, we assume the proxy s~\tilde{s} to be bounded in [0,1][0,1] and define the soft agreement as

SO(s~)≔𝔼ss~+(1−s)(1−s~).\soft(\tilde{s})\coloneqq\E s\tilde{s}+(1-s)(1-\tilde{s}).

For binary scores s~\tilde{s}, the soft agreement SO(s~)\soft(\tilde{s}) simply reduces to the agreement AG(s~)\agg(\tilde{s}). For non-binary proxy scores s~\tilde{s}, we interpret them as probability estimates, such that SO\soft equals the estimated probability of the real score ss. To make this interpretation valid, we focus on the recalibrated proxy R⁡(s~)=ℙ(s=1|s~){R(\tilde{s})=\Pr(s=1|\tilde{s})}. The following proposition suggests a way to generalize the condition AG≤b\agg\leq b:

Proposition 9.

Assume that b≥0.5b\geq 0.5. Then for any 0<ϵ≤10<\epsilon\leq 1, and any binary proxy s~\tilde{s} such that AG≥0.5\agg\geq 0.5 and ϵ⁡(1−b)≤(1−AG)\epsilon(1-b)\leq(1-\agg), the recalibrated proxy R⁡(s~)R(\tilde{s}) fulfills ϵ⁡(1−b)≤(1−SO(R⁡(s~)))\epsilon(1-b)\leq(1-\soft(R(\tilde{s}))).

For ϵ=1\epsilon=1, Proposition 9 states that if the agreement AG(s~)\agg(\tilde{s}) of a binary proxy s~\tilde{s} is below the evaluated model’s accuracy bb, the same is true for the soft accuracy SO(R⁡(s~))\soft(R(\tilde{s})) of the recalibrated proxy R⁡(s~)R(\tilde{s}). Based on this, we use ϵ⁡(1−b)≤(1−SO(R⁡(s~)))\epsilon(1-b)\leq(1-\soft(R(\tilde{s}))) to generalize the condition AG(s~)≤b\agg(\tilde{s})\leq b from Theorem 6, and prove:

Theorem 10.

For any non-constant proxy score s~\tilde{s} with ϵ⁡(1−b)≤(1−SO(R⁡(s~)))\epsilon(1-b)\leq(1-\soft(R(\tilde{s}))), we have ρ2​(s,s~)≤1−ϵ2\rho^{2}(s,\tilde{s})\leq 1-\frac{\epsilon}{2}. Correspondingly, the sample efficiency of PPI is bounded: τ⁡(θ^λ∗P​P)≤2ϵ\tau(\hat{\theta}^{PP}_{\lambda^{*}})\leq\frac{2}{\epsilon}.

We prove Proposition 9 and Theorem 10 in Appendices C.3 and C.4. Beyond generalizing to soft accuracy, these results also allow us to bound the sample efficiency factor in the binary case as 2ϵ\frac{2}{\epsilon} whenever the judge makes only ϵ\epsilon times as many errors as the evaluated model mm.

Experiments on MMLU

Using the prompt format from HELM, we extract LLama3.1-405b’s next-token predictions p~x\tilde{p}_{x} for all questions xx in MMLU. From these, we take the probabilities p~x​(t)\tilde{p}_{x}(t) corresponding to the four tokens t∈{A,B,C,D}≕Tt\in\{A,B,C,D\}\eqqcolon T representing the answers to question xx. We then renormalize them to ℙm′​(x)(t)=(p~x​(t))/(∑t′∈Tp~x​(t′))\Pr_{m^{\prime}(x)}(t)=(\tilde{p}_{x}(t))/(\sum_{t^{\prime}\in T}\tilde{p}_{x}(t^{\prime})) and define the proxy score s~​(x,m)\tilde{s}(x,m) as the probability ℙm′​(x)(m⁡(x))\Pr_{m^{\prime}(x)}(m(x)) assigned to the evaluated model’s answer m⁡(x)m(x), as described above.

Figure 4 shows the sample efficiency factor τ⁡(θ^λ∗P​P)\tau(\hat{\theta}^{PP}_{\lambda^{*}}) for PPI in the limit of infinite unlabeled data N→∞N\to\infty. As expected, using the non-binary proxy consistently improves sample efficiency. However, as suggested by Theorem 10, the sample efficiency factor τ⁡(θ^λ∗P​P)\tau(\hat{\theta}_{\lambda^{*}}^{PP}) remains below two when we use LLama3.1-405b to evaluate the stronger Claude 3.5 Sonnet. As in the previous experiments, the same is true for evaluating slightly weaker models such as GPT-4 or Gemini 1.5 Pro. This shows that our main claim of “no sample efficiency gains of more than a factor two at the frontier” is robust. That said, unlike in the binary case, the factor two is already (slightly) exceeded for LLaMa3-70b (which is 5% less accurate than LLama3.1-405b), rather than just for the much weaker LLama2-7b.

5 Related work

LLM-as-a-Judge.

With the success of large transformer-based language models, the idea of using model predictions to provide feedback for another model has become very popular. Initially, specialized fine-tuned models were used to provide training signals for a second model (Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022; Dorner et al., 2023). The approach was quickly expanded to using general purpose LLMs like GPT-4 (Achiam et al., 2023), not just for providing training signal but also for evaluating other models. This new paradigm, dubbed LLM-as-a-Judge, has been applied to evaluate a variety of model capabilities (Yu et al., 2023; Chiang and Lee, 2023; Fu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Weyssow et al., 2024; Raju et al., 2024; Vu et al., 2024; Kumar et al., 2024). In some cases, not just the ratings, but also the prompts given to evaluated models are designed by LLMs (Bai et al., 2024). LLM-as-a-Judge is often paired with another emerging paradigm for model evaluation: As generative tasks often do not have a single correct answer, models are evaluated in so-called arena benchmarks (Chiang et al., 2024), where different models’ responses to the same prompts are ranked to determine the best model. Beyond evaluating models, LLM judges have also been employed to evaluate red-teaming (Mazeika et al., 2024) and jailbreaks (Souly et al., 2024). The use of LLM judges rather than experts or crowd workers is often justified by high agreement rates (Gilardi et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024) between both types of judges. However, Thakur et al. (2024) find that seemingly high agreement does not necessarily imply accurate judge scores. In this work, we provide a theoretical justification for that finding and show that agreement is not necessarily a good indicator of judge quality, even when judge scores are debiased via PPI.

Bias in LLM judges.

LLM judges can be biased in numerous ways, making their evaluations unreliable: Their outputs often correlate poorly with expert annotations (Bavaresco et al., 2024; Koo et al., 2023). Models are known to rate their own outputs more favorably than the outputs of other models (Liu et al., 2023; Panickssery et al., 2024), prefer longer outputs and outputs containing lists, regardless of quality (Dubois et al., 2024b; Wei et al., 2024). They also exhibit choice-order bias (Dominguez-Olmedo et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2024) as well as a variety of other biases (Koo et al., 2023). While correcting for these known biases (Dubois et al., 2024a; Zheng et al., 2024) is an important first step, manually enumerating and correcting for all judge biases appears infeasible. As one potential alternative, Jung et al. (2024) propose to combat judge bias by having judges abstain based on their confidence. However, if abstention correlates with the evaluated model’s performance, this approach can introduce its own biases to model evaluations.

Debiasing methods.

Usually, the biases listed above are found by identifying patterns in how LLM judgments deviate from (a smaller set of) ground truth labels. Instead of trying to identify and fix specific biases, another line of work uses ground truth labels to directly estimate the bias an LLM judge introduces and correct for it. This approach was already suggested by Chaganty et al. (2018) for debiasing classic automated NLP metrics like BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) and ROUGE (Lin and Och, 2004). The authors find that their method, which is essentially equivalent to PPI, only improved data efficiency by around 10%10\% using 2018’s automated metrics. In addition, they show that their method has optimal worst-case variance. In comparison to their worst-case result, our Theorem 5 shows that θ^λ∗P​P\hat{\theta}^{PP}_{\lambda^{*}}is always optimal in our binary evaluation setting.

For modern LLM-based metrics, using PPI has been suggested by Boyeau et al. (2024) and Chatzi et al. (2024), and applied as part of more complicated evaluation pipelines (Saad-Falcon et al., 2023; Tyser et al., 2024). Furthermore, Fisch et al. (2024) combine PPI with stratified sampling for model evaluation. These works consistently show that PPI improves efficiency in terms of ground truth labels, but gains in effective sample size rarely exceed 50%50\% and are always below 100%100\%. Our upper bounds on the sample efficiency factor τmax\tau_{\max} show that gains larger than that are indeed unlikely, especially when evaluating state-of-the-art models.

6 Discussion

Our results show that for evaluating frontier models, LLM judges might fall short of the promise of largely replacing expert labelers: While doubling the effective sample size can be useful for practitioners, the order of magnitude of required ground truth labels remains the same with and without access to LLM judges. That said, there are ways to circumvent our negative results:

First, our results pertain to uniform sampling rather than more sophisticated sampling strategies. Approaches like stratified PPI (Fisch et al., 2024) might be able to obtain a somewhat better sample efficiency factor, for example by breaking the assumptions of Theorem 6 per-stratum. That said, Theorem 5 still applies per-stratum. Empirical results presented in Appendix B.3 suggest that at the frontier, stratified PPI rarely improves sample efficiency by more than a factor of two, compared to standard stratified sampling. Second, Theorem 6 only holds if the proxy s~\tilde{s} is less capable at predicting ss than the evaluated model mm is at its task. Thus, for tasks in which evaluation is substantially easier than the task itself, or tasks for which data to train a specialized evaluator is abundant, gains in sample efficiency of more than a factor two are possible even when evaluating models at the frontier. In addition, weaker models might find their way into many applications due to cost saving reasons, such that efficient evaluations of these models are still valuable.

Finally, we would like to reiterate that our results do not only apply to LLM judges, but any form of biased evaluators including (poorly instructed) crowdworkers. Whenever the crowdworker majority does not consistently agree with the desired ground truth labels, bias correction is required for valid evaluation results. Similarly, if the crowdworker majority vote is less accurate than the evaluated model, Theorem 6 implies that crowdworker labels are of low value compared to ground truth labels.

Appendix A Additional theoretical results

A.1 Balanced agreement rate as an alternative

Intuitively, high agreement fails to constrain the squared correlation ρ2\rho^{2} because predictors without any signal, such as constant predictors, can achieve high agreement. This is analogous to how accuracy can be misleading for imbalanced classification problems. In classification, this is solved by focusing on balanced accuracy instead. By analogy, we introduce the balanced agreement of s~\tilde{s} with ss as

BA(m)≔q⁡(m)+p⁡(m)2.\ba(m)\coloneqq\frac{q(m)+p(m)}{2}.

The next theorem confirms that controlling BA(m)\ba(m) yields meaningful lower bounds on the squared correlation.

Theorem 11.

For any value of BA(m)\ba(m), we have:

4b(m)(1−b(m))(2BA(m)−1)2≤ρ(s(m),s~(m))2≤|2BA(m)−1|.4b(m)(1-b(m))(2\ba(m)-1)^{2}\leq\rho(s(m),\tilde{s}(m))^{2}\leq|2\ba(m)-1|\,.

Theorem 11 is proven in Appendix C.5. It also provides another upper bound on sample efficiency gains from access to s~\tilde{s}: Whenever BA(m)\ba(m) is close to half, access to s~\tilde{s} can not improve sample efficiency by much and the sample efficiency factor τmax=11−ρ2\tau_{\max}=\frac{1}{1-\rho^{2}} is close to one. As a corollary, we show that whenever the proxy has reasonable balanced agreement, the minimum of the true positive rate pp and true negative rate qq upper bounds the squared correlation ρ2\rho^{2}:

Corollary 12.

Whenever BA(m)≥0.5\ba(m)\geq 0.5, we have

ρ​(s⁡(m),s~​(m))2≤min⁡{p⁡(m),q⁡(m)}.\rho(s(m),\tilde{s}(m))^{2}\leq\min\{p(m),q(m)\}.
Proof.

Given BA(m)≥0.5\ba(m)\geq 0.5, |2BA(m)−1||2\ba(m)-1| is maximized at the maximal value of BA(m)\ba(m). But given the constraint min⁡{p⁡(m),q⁡(m)}=r\min\{p(m),q(m)\}=r, that maximal value is r+12\frac{r+1}{2}. Inserting into Theorem 11 yields the result. ∎

Figure 5 shows the actual value of the maximal sample efficiency τmax\tau_{\max} and the corresponding lower and upper bounds derived from Theorem 11 for a variety of models. In line with our theoretical results, τmax\tau_{\max} lies consistently between the lower and upper bounds. Interestingly, the lower bound appears to be considerably tighter than the upper bound, that is, τmax\tau_{\max} is much closer to the lower bound than the upper bound throughout the experiments.

Appendix B Additional details on experiments

For MMLU, we obtain most model predictions from the HELM (Liang et al., 2023) leaderboard and focus on the top 10 models11 1 Cutoff date: 23.07.2024. As HELM does not document model uncertainty, and results for LLama3.1-405b were initially not available, we evaluated LLama3.1-405b in bf16 using 8 A100 GPUs and the accelerate library for offloading, ourselves. We use the prompting format from HELM and extract the predicted probabilities p~​(y)\tilde{p}(y) corresponding to the four tokens y∈Yy\in Y that represent the answer options. For our uncertainty experiment, we renormalize them, setting p⁡(y)=p~​(y)∑y′∈Yp~​(y′)p(y)=\frac{\tilde{p}(y)}{\sum_{y^{\prime}\in Y}\tilde{p}(y^{\prime})}.

For MT-Bench, we use the results for six models released by the benchmark’s authors (Zheng et al., 2024). For each triple consisting of two different models mm, m′m^{\prime} and a prompt xx there is a varying number of human expert judgments, as well as a judgment by GPT-4. We aggregate the expert judgments using a majority vote, and discard all triples for which the experts tied, or GPT-4’s judgment amounts to a tie. We then calculate the win-rate for model mm by averaging over all remaining triples that include mm. Note, that this is slightly different from the evaluation in the MT-Bench paper, where win-rates are calculated per model pair, and then averaged over models. MT-Bench also includes a follow-up prompt, with separate judgments for the first and second response. For simplicity, we focus on the first answer.

B.1 High agreement is not necessary for ranking

Proposition 2 indicates that a high agreement rate AG(m)\agg(m) is not sufficient for the proxy score s~\tilde{s} to yield similar model rankings as the real score ss. However, it turns out that high agreement is also not necessary for stable rankings: For binary classification with judge errors that are independent of the performance of different models, a sufficiently large sample size guarantees correct rankings as long as the error rate is below 50%50\% (Dorner and Hardt, 2024). We demonstrate this phenomenon in Figure 6. In that experiment, the judge reproduces the correct label 60%60\% of the time, but picks a random wrong label otherwise. Despite this judge’s low agreement with the correct labels, model rankings are preserved near-perfectly.

B.2 Additional results on TruthfulQA

Figure 7 shows additional results on TruthfulQA. As on MMLU, we extract model answers to the Q&A prompts from HELM22 2 We accessed the data on 14.11.2024, but it appears as if the leaderboard has not been updated to include recent models such as GPT-4. (Liang et al., 2023) and define the proxy score s~\tilde{s} using the judge’s answers m~​(x)\tilde{m}(x) as described in Section 2. We use the top three models in the leaderboard as judges, and consider evaluations of these as well as some worse-performing models. As predicted by our theory, the sample efficiency factor τmax\tau_{\max} is consistently below two when weaker models are used to evaluate stronger ones. Beyond that, the sample efficiency factor τmax\tau_{\max} even stays below two when we use the strongest model we considered (Palmyra-x) to judge the weakest (LLama2-7b).

B.3 Additional results on stratification

We consider a debiasing method for more sophisticated sampling strategies, namely stratified PPI (Fisch et al., 2024). Note that efficiency improvements from stratification occur independently from the model-as-judge regime. In order to disentangle gains from stratification from the gains of (stratified) PPI (Fisch et al., 2024), we therefore focus on the per-stratum sample efficiency factor τmax\tau_{\max}. Theorem 6 still holds per-stratum when applying stratified PPI, as long as the assumptions are valid for every stratum. It might however happen that the assumptions do not hold for every stratum, even if they are true globally: A judge model that is weaker than the evaluated model on average could still be stronger on certain strata, thus achieving a sample efficiency factor larger than two (on these strata).

Figure 8 suggests that this might be rare in practice: It shows the per-stratum sample efficiency factors τmax\tau_{\max} on MMLU, using subtasks as strata. Using GPT-4 to judge the stronger Claude (Figure 8(a)) and LLama3.1-405b (Figure 8(b)), the sample efficiency factors τmax\tau_{\max} vary significantly across strata. They are larger for most strata than the total (non-stratified) sample efficiency factor. However they consistently stay below two. Even when using the stronger LLama3.1-405b (Figure 8(d)) and Claude (Figure 8(c)) to judge GPT-4, sample efficiency gains above two remain rare: We only observe them in 6 out of 57 (Claude) and 1 out of 57 (LLama) cases.

C.2 Theorem 6

Proof.

To prove the theorem, we reparameterize to simplify the constraints, namely setting x=AG(m)≥0.5x=\agg(m)\geq 0.5 and δ=b⁡(m)−AG(m)≥0\delta=b(m)-\agg(m)\geq 0. For notational convenience, we also set q=q⁡(m)q=q(m). We then optimize the squared correlation ρ2\rho^{2} over the parameters in succession: At first, we take the derivative with respect to qq, finding two roots. Thus, the maximum of ρ2\rho^{2} with respect to qq is either at one of these roots or the boundary values for qq. We consider each candidate separately, and optimize over xx and δ\delta in a similar manner. This way, we enumerate all points q,x,δq,x,\delta that are candidates for the global maximum, i.e. all such points that are feasible, and either hit the boundary of a constraint or have zero derivative respectively, in all of the three variables.

We now delve into the details of the proof: Note that the agreement rate is given by AG(m)=(1−b)​q+bp\agg(m)=(1-b)q+bp. We therefore replace p⁡(m)=(b−1)​q+AG(m)b=(δ+x−1)​q+xbp(m)=\frac{(b-1)q+\agg(m)}{b}=\frac{(\delta+x-1)q+x}{b} and obtain a formula for ρ2\rho^{2} based on q,xq,x and δ:\delta:

C.4 Theorem 10

Proof.

First, we note that because the Mean squared error/Brier score is a proper scoring rule (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007), the Bayes-optimal predictor R(s~)\recal(\tilde{s}) minimizes the Mean squared error MSE(g⁡(s~),s)\mse(g(\tilde{s}),s) for all post-processing functions gg. At the same time, we have that the squared correlation ρ2​(s,s~)=R2​(s,f⁡(s~))=1−MSE(s,f⁡(s~))Var(s)\rho^{2}(s,\tilde{s})=R^{2}(s,f(\tilde{s}))=1-\frac{\mse(s,f(\tilde{s}))}{\V(s)} falls monotonously in MSE(s,f⁡(s~))\mse(s,f(\tilde{s})), where ff is the affine transformation with the smallest value of MSE(s,f⁡(s~))\mse(s,f(\tilde{s})) (Larsen and Marx, 2005). This means that the Bayes-optimal predictor R(s~)\recal(\tilde{s}) fulfills ρ2​(s,R(s~))≥ρ2​(s,s~)\rho^{2}({s,\recal(\tilde{s})})\geq\rho^{2}(s,{\tilde{s}}). As the Bayes-optimal predictor is calibrated, it is sufficient to prove our upper bound for calibrated scores s~\tilde{s} (i.e. scores s~\tilde{s} such that ℙ(s=1|s~=γ)=γ\Pr(s=1|\tilde{s}=\gamma)=\gamma for all γ∈[0,1]\gamma\in[0,1]).

In the following, we assume s~\tilde{s} to be calibrated. This means that

MSE(s,s~)=𝔼(s−s~)2=∫01((1−s~)2​s~+s~2​(1−s~))​dP​(s~)=∫01(1−s~)​s~​dP​(s~),\mse(s,\tilde{s})=\E(s-\tilde{s})^{2}=\int_{0}^{1}((1-\tilde{s})^{2}\tilde{s}+\tilde{s}^{2}(1-\tilde{s}))dP(\tilde{s})=\int_{0}^{1}(1-\tilde{s})\tilde{s}dP(\tilde{s}),

where we use that because of calibration, conditional on a prediction s~\tilde{s}, ss is one and the squared error is (1−s~)2(1-\tilde{s})^{2} with probability s~\tilde{s}. Similarly, the squared error is s~2\tilde{s}^{2} with probability (1−s~)(1-\tilde{s}).

At the same time, the soft accuracy of s~\tilde{s} equals

SO=∫01(s~2+(1−s~)2)​dP​(s~)=∫01(2​s~​(s~−1)+1)​dP​(s~)\soft=\int_{0}^{1}(\tilde{s}^{2}+(1-\tilde{s})^{2})dP(\tilde{s})=\int_{0}^{1}(2\tilde{s}(\tilde{s}-1)+1)dP(\tilde{s})

for calibrated scores s~\tilde{s}, as s=1s=1 yields a score of s~\tilde{s} and happens with probability s~\tilde{s}, and s=0s=0 happens with probability (1−s~)(1-\tilde{s}) and gets a score of 1−s~1-\tilde{s}.

By the linearity of the integral, this implies that

SO=1−2MSE\soft=1-2\mse

or

MSE=1−SO2.\mse=\frac{1-\soft}{2}.

As s~\tilde{s} is Bayes-optimal with respect to itself, the optimal affine transformation in terms of M​S​EMSE is just the identity. Thus, we have that

ρ2​(s,s~)=R2​(s~,s)=1−MSEVar(s)=1−1−SO2b⁡(1−b)=1−1−SO2​b​(1−b).\rho^{2}(s,\tilde{s})=R^{2}(\tilde{s},s)=1-\frac{\mse}{\V(s)}=1-\frac{\frac{1-\soft}{2}}{b(1-b)}=1-\frac{1-\soft}{2b(1-b)}.

This is decreasing in 1−SO1-\soft and thus maximized at the minimal value of 1−SO1-\soft, which equals ϵ⁡(1−b)\epsilon(1-b) by assumption. Inserting yields

ρ2​(s~,s)≤1−ϵ⁡(1−b)2​b​(1−b)=1−ϵ2​b.\rho^{2}(\tilde{s},s)\leq 1-\frac{\epsilon(1-b)}{2b(1-b)}=1-\frac{\epsilon}{2b}.

This is increasing in bb and thus maximized at b=1b=1, where we have

ρ2​(s~,s)≤1−ϵ2.\rho^{2}(\tilde{s},s)\leq 1-\frac{\epsilon}{2}.
